planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into deep, loose, stone-free soil; Takinogawa needs at least 18-24 inches of unobstructed depth for its long taproot to develop straight.

directions: Direct sow into deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun; Takinogawa is the standard Japanese market variety of burdock, grown as an annual for its long, slender, aromatic taproot that can reach 2-3 feet if the soil allows. Loosen the bed a full spade's depth or more before sowing, since any obstruction causes the root to fork or twist. Harvest in fall once roots reach full size, and use the earthy, mildly sweet root in classic preparations like kinpira gobo and other simmered dishes.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost danger passes. Fushimi is one of the traditional Kyo-yasai vegetables of Kyoto.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Fushimi is one of the Kyo-yasai, the traditional heirloom vegetables of Kyoto, producing thin-walled, glossy, slender tapered pods up to 6 inches long with a mild heat (1,000-2,500 SHU). The productive plants bear continuously through the season; harvest pods green for the best texture, especially for tempura, where Fushimi's thin walls fry up light and crisp. It performs well in both garden rows and containers.

planting.note: Sow thickly on a damp sprouting tray or shallow soil indoors; Kaiware grows year-round indoors and is harvested as a sprout, not a mature root crop.

directions: Sow thickly on a damp sprouting tray or shallow soil indoors, out of direct hot sun; Kaiware is daikon radish grown specifically as a sprout rather than for its root, harvested in just 5-10 days once the cotyledons unfurl above the thin white stems. It carries a spicy, sharp, radish-forward flavor that makes it a classic garnish for sashimi and sushi and a crunchy addition to salads and sandwiches. Keep the growing medium consistently moist and harvest by cutting at the base once the sprouts reach 2-4 inches tall, well before any true leaves fully develop.

common_name: Citrus F1 Chinese Cabbage (Orange-Interior Napa Cabbage)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop into fertile, moisture-retentive soil; Citrus is a cool-season biennial grown as an annual and bolts quickly in hot weather.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Citrus is a Johnny's Selected Seeds hybrid napa cabbage forming a tall, barrel-shaped head around 11 inches tall and 5.5-6 pounds, distinguished by a striking deep-orange interior and orange-ringed cut stems rather than the usual pale yellow-green. It performs best as a fall crop sown in late summer, since the cool-season biennial bolts quickly if grown through summer heat. Use it fresh in slaws and salads or fermented into a colorfully different kimchi.

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Early Hakucho ripens with unusually uniform timing, suited to a single-pass harvest.

directions: Direct sow in full sun into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Early Hakucho is an extra-early, compact bush edamame maturing in just 75 days, among the earliest soybean cultivars grown for fresh eating. Its pods ripen with unusually uniform timing, making it well suited to a single efficient harvest pass rather than picking over several weeks, which is also convenient for home freezing. The beans carry a sweet, creamy flavor typical of the best edamame types; blanch pods briefly in salted water and pop the beans free to eat.

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Agate is a compact heirloom bush type with unusually high yield for its small seed size.

directions: Direct sow in full sun into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Agate is a 1920s Japan-origin heirloom edamame with small olive-green seeds marked by a distinctive brown 'saddle' patch. The compact bush habit belies a very high yield for its small seed size, maturing in roughly 65-85 days depending on climate. Pods carry a buttery, rich flavor prized by edamame enthusiasts; blanch briefly in salted water and pop the beans free of the pod to eat warm or chilled.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring or late summer into fertile, loose soil; Yeolmu is harvested fast, within three to six weeks, for both its tender greens and slim root together.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, loose soil in full sun; Yeolmu is a fast-growing Korean radish type harvested young, in just three to six weeks, prized for its tender peppery greens eaten together with the slim immature root rather than a mature root alone. It is the namesake ingredient of summer yeolmu-kimchi, a quick-fermented dish traditionally served with cold noodles in hot weather. Sow successively through spring and late summer for a continuous supply, since the whole point of this cultivar is harvesting it young and fast rather than letting it mature into a full-size radish.

planting.note: Direct sow into warm, moist soil or a shallow water tray well after last frost; Bamboo Leaf is more heat-tolerant and needs less standing water than the broad-leaf Chinese type.

directions: Direct sow into warm, consistently moist soil or a shallow water tray in full sun; Bamboo Leaf is a narrow-leaf type of water spinach with small, slender arrowhead-shaped leaves on long hollow stems, more heat-tolerant and less dependent on standing water than the broad-leaf Chinese type grown in wet paddies. It is a tropical perennial grown as a warm-season annual outside zones 9-11, ready to begin cutting within 30-45 days and resprouting readily for repeated harvests through summer. Stir-fry quickly with garlic and chile, the classic Thai preparation phak bung fai daeng, to preserve its crisp texture.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Nira regrows after cutting, allowing several harvests per season.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this broad-leaf nira selection carries wider, flatter leaves than standard garlic chives, prized in Chinese and Japanese stir-fries and dumpling fillings for its stronger texture and flavor. It is a hardy clumping perennial that regrows readily after cutting, supporting several harvests through a single growing season from one planting. Established clumps can be divided every few years in spring both to propagate and to keep the planting vigorous.
